claim: Protozoan parasites of the Leishmania donovani complex – L. donovani and L. infantum – cause the fatal disease visceral leishmaniasis.
source: Protozoan parasites of the Leishmania donovani complex – L. donovani and L. infantum – cause the fatal disease visceral leishmaniasis.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about the causative agents of visceral leishmaniasis.

claim: The study presents the first comprehensive genome-wide global study of the L. donovani complex, with 151 cultured field isolates representing most of the geographical distribution.
source: We present the first comprehensive genome-wide global study, with 151 cultured field isolates representing most of the geographical distribution.
evidence: The manuscript describes the scope and novelty of the study conducted.

claim: L. donovani isolates separated into five groups that largely coincide with geographical origin but vary greatly in diversity.
source: L. donovani isolates separated into five groups that largely coincide with geographical origin but vary greatly in diversity.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the phylogenetic analysis presented in the study.

claim: The majority of L. infantum samples fell into one globally-distributed group with little diversity.
source: In contrast, the majority of L. infantum samples fell into one globally-distributed group with little diversity.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the phylogenetic analysis presented in the study.

claim: Several hybrid lineages complicate the population structure of the L. donovani complex.
source: This picture is complicated by several hybrid lineages.
evidence: The study identified hybrid lineages through genomic analysis.

claim: Identified genetic groups vary in heterozygosity and levels of linkage, suggesting different recombination histories.
source: Identified genetic groups vary in heterozygosity and levels of linkage, suggesting different recombination histories.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed patterns of heterozygosity and linkage disequilibrium in the data.

claim: The study characterizes chromosome-specific patterns of aneuploidy in the L. donovani complex.
source: We characterise chromosome-specific patterns of aneuploidy and identified extensive structural variation, including known and suspected drug resistance loci.
evidence: The manuscript presents analysis of chromosome copy number variation across isolates.

claim: The study identified extensive structural variation, including known and suspected drug resistance loci.
source: We characterise chromosome-specific patterns of aneuploidy and identified extensive structural variation, including known and suspected drug resistance loci.
evidence: The manuscript describes identification of structural variants and their association with drug resistance.

claim: The genus Leishmania comprises more than 20 species of protozoan parasites that cause the neglected tropical disease leishmaniasis in humans and other mammalian hosts.
source: The genus Leishmania is a group of more than 20 species of protozoan parasites that cause the neglected tropical disease leishmaniasis in humans, but also infect other mammalian hosts.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the Leishmania genus.

claim: Leishmaniasis is transmitted by phlebotomine sandflies.
source: Leishmaniasis is transmitted by phlebotomine sandflies and exists in four main clinical conditions: cutaneous leishmaniasis (CL), seen as single and multiple cutaneous lesions; mucocutaneous leishmaniasis (MCL), presenting in mucosal tissue; diffuse cutaneous leishmaniasis (DCL), seen as multiple nodular cutaneous lesions covering much of the body; and visceral leishmaniasis (VL, also known as kala-azar), affecting internal organs.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about leishmaniasis transmission.

claim: Leishmaniasis exists in four main clinical conditions: cutaneous leishmaniasis (CL), mucocutaneous leishmaniasis (MCL), diffuse cutaneous leishmaniasis (DCL), and visceral leishmaniasis (VL).
source: Leishmaniasis is transmitted by phlebotomine sandflies and exists in four main clinical conditions: cutaneous leishmaniasis (CL), seen as single and multiple cutaneous lesions; mucocutaneous leishmaniasis (MCL), presenting in mucosal tissue; diffuse cutaneous leishmaniasis (DCL), seen as multiple nodular cutaneous lesions covering much of the body; and visceral leishmaniasis (VL, also known as kala-azar), affecting internal organs.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the clinical manifestations of leishmaniasis.

claim: Disease incidence per year is estimated at 0.9 to 1.6 million new cases, mostly of cutaneous leishmaniasis.
source: Disease incidence per year is estimated at 0.9 to 1.6 million new cases, mostly of CL, and up to 90,000 new cases per year of VL are associated with a 10% mortality rate (Alvar et al., 2012; Burza et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to epidemiological studies.

claim: Up to 90,000 new cases per year of visceral leishmaniasis are associated with a 10% mortality rate.
source: Disease incidence per year is estimated at 0.9 to 1.6 million new cases, mostly of CL, and up to 90,000 new cases per year of VL are associated with a 10% mortality rate (Alvar et al., 2012; Burza et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to epidemiological studies.

claim: The form of leishmaniasis disease is largely driven by the species of Leishmania causing the infection but is further influenced by vector biology and host factors, importantly by host immune status.
source: The form of the disease is largely driven by the species of Leishmania causing the infection but is further influenced by vector biology and host factors, importantly by host immune status (Burza et al., 2018; McCall et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: In the mammalian host, Leishmania parasites are intracellular, residing mainly in long lived macrophages.
source: In the mammalian host, parasites are intracellular, residing mainly in long lived macrophages.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about Leishmania biology.

claim: In visceral leishmaniasis, parasites infect the spleen, liver, bone marrow and lymph nodes, leading to splenomegaly and hepatomegaly.
source: In the most severe visceral form, parasites infect the spleen, liver, bone marrow and lymph nodes, leading to splenomegaly and hepatomegaly.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about visceral leishmaniasis pathology.

claim: Visceral leishmaniasis results in a range of symptoms including frequent anaemia, thrombocytopenia and neutropenia, and common secondary infections which are often fatal without successful treatment.
source: This results in a range of symptoms including frequent anaemia, thrombocytopenia and neutropenia, and common secondary infections which are often fatal without successful treatment (for review see: Rodrigues et al., 2016; Burza et al., 2018), although most infections remain asymptomatic (Ostyn et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to review articles and research studies.

claim: Most Leishmania infections remain asymptomatic.
source: This results in a range of symptoms including frequent anaemia, thrombocytopenia and neutropenia, and common secondary infections which are often fatal without successful treatment (for review see: Rodrigues et al., 2016; Burza et al., 2018), although most infections remain asymptomatic (Ostyn et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a research study.

claim: The key species responsible for visceral leishmaniasis are L. donovani and L. infantum.
source: The key species responsible for VL are L. donovani and L. infantum (see reviews McCall et al., 2013; Burza et al., 2018), which together form the L. donovani species complex.
evidence: This is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: Both L. donovani and L. infantum mainly cause visceral leishmaniasis, but for each species atypical cutaneous presentations are common in some foci.
source: Both species mainly cause VL, but for each species atypical cutaneous presentations are common in some foci (reviewed in Thakur et al., 2018; for example, Guerbouj et al., 2001; Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to review articles and research studies.

claim: Post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis (PKDL) is a common sequel to visceral leishmaniasis that manifests with dermatological symptoms appearing after apparent cure of the visceral infection.
source: Post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis (PKDL), is a common sequel to VL that manifests with dermatological symptoms appearing after apparent cure of the visceral infection.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about PKDL.

claim: PKDL is mainly seen on the Indian subcontinent and north-eastern and eastern Africa following infections caused by L. donovani.
source: PKDL is mainly seen on the Indian subcontinent and north-eastern and eastern Africa following infections caused by L. donovani (Zijlstra et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a research study.

claim: L. donovani is considered to be largely anthroponotic even though the parasites can be encountered in animals.
source: L. donovani is considered to be largely anthroponotic even though the parasites can be encountered in animals (Bhattarai et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a research study.

claim: L. infantum causes a zoonotic disease, where dogs are the major domestic reservoir but a range of wild mammals can also be involved in transmission.
source: In contrast, L. infantum – like most Leishmania species – causes a zoonotic disease, where dogs are the major domestic reservoir but a range of wild mammals can also be involved in transmission (Díaz-Sáez et al., 2014; Quinnell and Courtenay, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to research studies.

claim: L. donovani has major foci in the Indian subcontinent and East Africa.
source: Both species are widespread across the globe, with major foci in the Indian subcontinent and East Africa for L. donovani, the Mediterranean region and the Middle East for L. infantum, and China for both species (Lun et al., 2015; Lysenko, 1971; Ready, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to research studies.

claim: L. infantum has major foci in the Mediterranean region and the Middle East.
source: Both species are widespread across the globe, with major foci in the Indian subcontinent and East Africa for L. donovani, the Mediterranean region and the Middle East for L. infantum, and China for both species (Lun et al., 2015; Lysenko, 1971; Ready, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to research studies.

claim: Both L. donovani and L. infantum are present in China.
source: Both species are widespread across the globe, with major foci in the Indian subcontinent and East Africa for L. donovani, the Mediterranean region and the Middle East for L. infantum, and China for both species (Lun et al., 2015; Lysenko, 1971; Ready, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to research studies.

claim: L. infantum spread to the New World via European migration during the 15th or 16th Century.
source: L. infantum has also more recently spread to the New World, via European migration during the 15th or 16th Century (Leblois et al., 2011), where it was sometimes described as a third species, L. chagasi.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a research study.

claim: L. infantum in the New World was sometimes described as a third species, L. chagasi.
source: L. infantum has also more recently spread to the New World, via European migration during the 15th or 16th Century (Leblois et al., 2011), where it was sometimes described as a third species, L. chagasi.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about Leishmania taxonomy.

claim: Leishmaniasis caused by parasites of the L. donovani complex differs across and even within geographical locations in the nature and severity of clinical symptoms.
source: Leishmaniasis caused by parasites of the L. donovani complex differs across and even within geographical locations in the nature and severity of clinical symptoms (e.g. Guerbouj et al., 2001; Zhang et al., 2014; Thakur et al., 2018) and in the species of phlebotomine sandflies that act as vectors (Alemayehu and Alemayehu, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to research studies.

claim: Leishmaniasis caused by parasites of the L. donovani complex differs in the species of phlebotomine sandflies that act as vectors.
source: Leishmaniasis caused by parasites of the L. donovani complex differs across and even within geographical locations in the nature and severity of clinical symptoms (e.g. Guerbouj et al., 2001; Zhang et al., 2014; Thakur et al., 2018) and in the species of phlebotomine sandflies that act as vectors (Alemayehu and Alemayehu, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a research study.

claim: Leishmania has two unusual genomic features that influence its genetics: mosaic aneuploidy and a complex and predominantly clonal life cycle.
source: Leishmania has two unusual genomic features that influence its genetics, including mosaic aneuploidy and a complex and predominantly clonal life cycle.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about Leishmania genetics.

claim: Aneuploidy is the phenomenon where individual chromosomes within a cell are of different copy numbers.
source: Aneuploidy is the phenomenon where individual chromosomes within a cell are of different copy numbers, and mosaic aneuploidy is where the pattern of chromosome dosage varies between cells of a clonal population (Bastien et al., 1990; Sterkers et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a definition supported by citations to research studies.

claim: Mosaic aneuploidy is where the pattern of chromosome dosage varies between cells of a clonal population.
source: Aneuploidy is the phenomenon where individual chromosomes within a cell are of different copy numbers, and mosaic aneuploidy is where the pattern of chromosome dosage varies between cells of a clonal population (Bastien et al., 1990; Sterkers et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a definition supported by citations to research studies.

claim: Genome sequencing studies have shown extensive aneuploidy in cultured Leishmania field isolates.
source: Genome sequencing studies have shown extensive aneuploidy in cultured Leishmania field isolates (e.g. Downing et al., 2011; Rogers et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2014; Imamura et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple research studies.

claim: Variation in chromosome dosage appears to be greater in in vitro than in vivo in animal models or human tissues.
source: Variation in chromosome dosage appears to be greater in in vitro than in vivo in animal models (Dumetz et al., 2017) or human tissues (Domagalska et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to research studies.

claim: Only a few studies have directly investigated mosaicism between cells in Leishmania and these found it to be extensive both in vitro and in vivo.
source: Only a few studies have directly investigated mosaicism between cells and these found it to be extensive both in vitro (Sterkers et al., 2011; Lachaud et al., 2014) and in vivo (Prieto Barja et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to research studies.

claim: Reproduction in Leishmania was originally thought to be predominantly clonal and this is still assumed to be the only mode of reproduction for the intracellular amastigotes found in the mammalian host.
source: Reproduction was originally thought to be predominantly clonal and this is still assumed to be the only mode of reproduction for the intracellular amastigotes found in the mammalian host.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about Leishmania reproduction.

claim: A number of studies have shown that hybridisation can occur during passage in the sandfly vector in Leishmania.
source: A number of studies have shown that hybridisation can occur during passage in the sandfly vector. This was demonstrated experimentally (e.g. Akopyants et al., 2009; Romano et al., 2014; Inbar et al., 2019) also showing evidence of meiosis (Inbar et al., 2019) and in field isolates through recombination-like signatures (Cotton et al., 2019; Rogers et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple research studies.

claim: Experimental studies have shown evidence of meiosis in Leishmania.
source: A number of studies have shown that hybridisation can occur during passage in the sandfly vector. This was demonstrated experimentally (e.g. Akopyants et al., 2009; Romano et al., 2014; Inbar et al., 2019) also showing evidence of meiosis (Inbar et al., 2019) and in field isolates through recombination-like signatures (Cotton et al., 2019; Rogers et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a research study.

claim: The incidence of sexual reproduction in natural Leishmania populations is still unclear.
source: However, the incidence of sexual reproduction in natural populations is still unclear (Ramírez and Llewellyn, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a research study.

claim: Isoenzyme typing dominated the description of Leishmania populations for at least 25 years but suffered from a critical lack of resolution, leading to convergent signals.
source: Difficult and laborious isoenzyme typing (Rioux et al., 1990) dominated the description of Leishmania populations for at least 25 years (Schönian et al., 2011) but suffered from a critical lack of resolution, leading to convergent signals (Jamjoom et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to research studies.

claim: More recent typing schemes using multi-locus sequence typing (MLST) or multi locus microsatellite typing (MLMT) improved the resolution of Leishmania phylogenies and enabled population genetic analyses.
source: More recent typing schemes, using variation at small numbers of genetic loci (multi-locus sequence typing, MLST) or microsatellite repeats (multi locus microsatellite typing, MLMT) improved the resolution of Leishmania phylogenies and enabled population genetic analyses (Gouzelou et al., 2012; Herrera et al., 2017; Kuhls et al., 2007; Schönian et al., 2011) but are hard to compare when using different marker sets (Schönian et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to research studies.

claim: MLST and MLMT typing schemes are hard to compare when using different marker sets.
source: More recent typing schemes, using variation at small numbers of genetic loci (multi-locus sequence typing, MLST) or microsatellite repeats (multi locus microsatellite typing, MLMT) improved the resolution of Leishmania phylogenies and enabled population genetic analyses (Gouzelou et al., 2012; Herrera et al., 2017; Kuhls et al., 2007; Schönian et al., 2011) but are hard to compare when using different marker sets (Schönian et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a research study.

claim: Genome-wide polymorphism data offers much greater resolution than previous typing methods for Leishmania.
source: In contrast, genome-wide polymorphism data offers much greater resolution (Downing et al., 2011; Rogers et al., 2014), provides richer information on aneuploidy and other classes of variants, that is SNPs, small indels and structural variants, and enables insights into gene function from genome-wide studies of selection and association mapping (Carnielli et al., 2018; Downing et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to research studies.

claim: Genome-wide polymorphism data provides richer information on aneuploidy and other classes of variants (SNPs, small indels and structural variants) in Leishmania.
source: In contrast, genome-wide polymorphism data offers much greater resolution (Downing et al., 2011; Rogers et al., 2014), provides richer information on aneuploidy and other classes of variants, that is SNPs, small indels and structural variants, and enables insights into gene function from genome-wide studies of selection and association mapping (Carnielli et al., 2018; Downing et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to research studies.

claim: Genome-wide polymorphism data enables insights into gene function from genome-wide studies of selection and association mapping in Leishmania.
source: In contrast, genome-wide polymorphism data offers much greater resolution (Downing et al., 2011; Rogers et al., 2014), provides richer information on aneuploidy and other classes of variants, that is SNPs, small indels and structural variants, and enables insights into gene function from genome-wide studies of selection and association mapping (Carnielli et al., 2018; Downing et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to research studies.

claim: Advances in DNA sequencing technology together with the availability of reference genome assemblies for most clinically important Leishmania species make it feasible to sequence collections of isolates and determine genetic variants genome-wide.
source: Moreover, advances in DNA sequencing technology together with the availability of reference genome assemblies for most of the clinically important species (Downing et al., 2011; González-de la Fuente et al., 2019; Peacock et al., 2007; Real et al., 2013; Rogers et al., 2011) in public databases (Aslett et al., 2010) now make it feasible to sequence collections of isolates and determine genetic variants genome-wide.
evidence: This is supported by citations to research studies and databases.

claim: Several genomic studies on the L. donovani complex have been conducted in geographically restricted regions including Nepal, Turkey, the Indian subcontinent, Ethiopia and Brazil.
source: Several studies on the L. donovani complex have applied such an approach including foci in Nepal (16 isolates, Downing et al., 2011), Turkey (12 isolates, Rogers et al., 2014), the Indian subcontinent (204 isolates, Imamura et al., 2016), Ethiopia (41 isolates from 16 patients, Zackay et al., 2018) and Brazil (20 and 26 isolates, respectively, Teixeira et al., 2017; Carnielli et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple research studies.

claim: Genomic studies to date on the L. donovani complex have addressed genome-wide diversity in geographically restricted regions, leaving global genome diversity in the species complex unknown.
source: However, genomic studies to date have addressed genome-wide diversity in geographically restricted regions, leaving global genome diversity in the species complex unknown.
evidence: This is an inference based on the review of previous studies.

claim: The study generated paired-end Illumina whole-genome sequence data from promastigote cultures of 97 isolates from the L. donovani complex.
source: We generated paired-end Illumina whole-genome sequence data from promastigote cultures of 97 isolates from the L. donovani complex.
evidence: This describes the data generation methods used in the study.

claim: The sequence data resulted in a median haploid genome coverage ranging between 10 and 88 (median = 27) when mapped against the reference genome assembly of L. infantum JPCM5.
source: These sequence data resulted in a median haploid genome coverage ranging between 10 and 88 (median = 27) when mapped against the reference genome assembly of L. infantum JPCM5 (MCAN/ES/98/LLM-724; Peacock et al., 2007).
evidence: This describes the sequencing coverage achieved in the study.

claim: The study combined newly generated data with subsets of previously published sequence data to represent previously sampled genetic and geographic diversity, resulting in a total of 151 isolates.
source: These data were combined with subsets of previously published sequence data of strains of the L. donovani complex to represent previously sampled genetic as well as geographic diversity including parasites from Turkey (N = 11, Rogers et al., 2014), Sri Lanka (N = 2, Zhang et al., 2014), Spain (N = 1, Peacock et al., 2007), Ethiopia (N = 1, Rogers et al., 2011); N = 6, Zackay et al., 2018) and a subset of the extensive dataset available from the Indian subcontinent (N = 33, Imamura et al., 2016) resulting in a total of 151 isolates (Supplementary file 1, visualised at https://microreact.org/project/_FWlYSTGf; Argimón et al., 2016).
evidence: This describes the data compilation approach used in the study.

claim: Accurate SNP variants were identified across 87.8% of the reference genome with a genotype quality of at least 10 (median = 99).
source: Accurate SNP variants were identified across 87.8% of the reference genome with a genotype quality of at least 10 (median = 99), indicating a < 0.1 (median = ~10−10) probability of an incorrect genotype call.
evidence: This describes the SNP calling results from the study.

claim: The remaining 12.2% of the reference genome could not be assayed as short reads could not be uniquely mapped to repetitive parts of the genome.
source: The remaining 12.2% could not be assayed as short reads could not be uniquely mapped to repetitive parts of the genome.
evidence: This describes a limitation of the sequencing approach used.

claim: The study identified a total of 395,624 SNP sites out of the 32 Mb reference assembly.
source: This identified a total of 395,624 SNP sites out of the 32 Mb reference assembly.
evidence: This describes the total number of SNPs identified in the study.

claim: The study used sequence data to infer extensive gene copy-number variation (91.5% of genes varied in dosage; 7,625/8,330 genes).
source: We also used these sequence data to infer extensive gene copy-number variation (91.5% of genes varied in dosage; 7,625/8,330 genes) and larger genome structure variation, including copy numbers of individual chromosomes (aneuploidy) that is common in Leishmania.
evidence: This describes the copy number variation analysis results from the study.

claim: Phylogenetic reconstruction based on whole-genome SNP variation clearly separated L. infantum from L. donovani strains.
source: Phylogenetic reconstruction based on whole-genome SNP variation clearly separated L. infantum from L. donovani strains.
evidence: This describes a primary finding from the phylogenetic analysis.

claim: There is a strong signal of isolation-by-distance between countries for L. donovani (0.76, p-value<=0.0001, Mantel test).
source: L. donovani separated into five major groups that coincide with geographic origin (Figure 1A–B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1) and show a strong signal of isolation-by-distance (IBD) between countries (0.76, p-value<=0.0001, Mantel test, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This describes a statistical result from the population genetic analysis.

claim: Groups within L. donovani showed similar levels of divergence as between the two species L. donovani and L. infantum.
source: While the inferred root of the phylogeny is between L. infantum and L. donovani, groups within L. donovani showed similar levels of divergence as between the two species, with the deepest branches within L. donovani in East Africa.
evidence: This is an observation from the phylogenetic analysis.

claim: The deepest branches within L. donovani are in East Africa.
source: While the inferred root of the phylogeny is between L. infantum and L. donovani, groups within L. donovani showed similar levels of divergence as between the two species, with the deepest branches within L. donovani in East Africa.
evidence: This is an observation from the phylogenetic analysis.

claim: The largest L. donovani group (Ldon1) includes samples from the Indian subcontinent and displays strikingly little diversity.
source: The largest L. donovani group in our collection, Ldon1, included samples from the Indian subcontinent, and could be further divided into two subgroups that separate samples from India, Nepal and Bangladesh from three samples of Sri Lankan origin; both subgroups displayed strikingly little diversity.
evidence: This describes a finding from the phylogenetic and diversity analysis.

claim: The Ldon1 group can be further divided into two subgroups that separate samples from India, Nepal and Bangladesh from three samples of Sri Lankan origin.
source: The largest L. donovani group in our collection, Ldon1, included samples from the Indian subcontinent, and could be further divided into two subgroups that separate samples from India, Nepal and Bangladesh from three samples of Sri Lankan origin; both subgroups displayed strikingly little diversity.
evidence: This describes a finding from the phylogenetic analysis.

claim: The Ldon1 group represents the 'core group' of strains circulating in the Indian subcontinent as identified by previous genomic work.
source: The large number of isolates in Ldon1 is due to the extensive previous genomic work in this population (Downing et al., 2011; Imamura et al., 2016), which identified this as the 'core group' of strains circulating in the Indian subcontinent.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: The Ldon2 group is restricted to the Nepali highlands and includes the more divergent sample BPK512A1.
source: The genetically and geographically closest group, Ldon2, was restricted to the Nepali highlands and also includes the more divergent sample, BPK512A1 (Ldon2 is the ISC1 group of Imamura et al., 2016).
evidence: This describes a finding from the phylogenetic analysis.

claim: The Ldon2 group corresponds to the ISC1 group identified by Imamura et al., 2016.
source: The genetically and geographically closest group, Ldon2, was restricted to the Nepali highlands and also includes the more divergent sample, BPK512A1 (Ldon2 is the ISC1 group of Imamura et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous research study.

claim: The Ldon4 group comprises parasites from the Middle East (Iraq and Saudi Arabia) and Ethiopia and is far more diverse.
source: The latter isolate shared sequence similarity with a far more diverse group, Ldon4, of parasites from the Middle East (Iraq and Saudi Arabia) and Ethiopia (Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes a finding from the phylogenetic and diversity analysis.

claim: Admixture analysis identified three additional samples (from Sudan and Israel) to be of mixed origin between groups Ldon3 and Ldon4.
source: Admixture analysis identified three additional samples (from Sudan and Israel), to be of mixed origin between groups Ldon3 and Ldon4.
evidence: This describes a finding from the admixture analysis.

claim: The Ldon3 group is restricted to Sudan and northern Ethiopia with an outlier sampled in Malta likely representing an imported case.
source: The Ldon3 group is restricted to Sudan and northern Ethiopia and an outlier sampled in Malta likely represents an imported case.
evidence: This describes a finding from the phylogenetic analysis with an inference about the Malta sample.

claim: Group Ldon5 displays little diversity and is mainly confined to Southern Ethiopia and Kenya.
source: Group Ldon5 displayed little diversity and is mainly confined to Southern Ethiopia and Kenya, with the rift valley in Ethiopia presumably restricting genetic exchange with Ldon3 through different sandfly vectors (Gebre-Michael et al., 2010; Gebre-Michael and Lane, 1996).
evidence: This describes a finding from the phylogenetic and diversity analysis.

claim: The rift valley in Ethiopia presumably restricts genetic exchange between Ldon3 and Ldon5 through different sandfly vectors.
source: Group Ldon5 displayed little diversity and is mainly confined to Southern Ethiopia and Kenya, with the rift valley in Ethiopia presumably restricting genetic exchange with Ldon3 through different sandfly vectors (Gebre-Michael et al., 2010; Gebre-Michael and Lane, 1996).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations to research studies on sandfly vectors.

claim: A single outlier from the Ldon5 group (LRC-L51p) was sampled in India and presumably represents an imported case of African origin.
source: A single outlier from this group, LRC-L51p, was sampled in India and again presumably represents an imported case of African origin.
evidence: This is an inference based on the phylogenetic placement of the sample.

claim: Most L. infantum samples cluster into a single group (Linf1) with relatively little diversity but a broad geographical distribution including Central Asia, the Mediterranean Region and Latin America.
source: In contrast, most of the samples of L. infantum clustered into a single group, Linf1, with relatively little diversity but a broad geographical distribution including Central Asia, the Mediterranean Region and Latin America but also very distinct lineages from the Western Mediterranean (Figure 1A–B).
evidence: This describes a finding from the phylogenetic and diversity analysis.

claim: Admixture analysis divided the Linf1 group into two to three subgroups, separating samples from China, Uzbekistan and a single Israeli isolate from two groups that both include samples from the Mediterranean region and Central/South America.
source: Admixture analysis using different numbers of total populations (K) divided the Linf1 group into two to three subgroups, separating samples from China, Uzbekistan and a single Israeli isolate, from two groups that both include samples from the Mediterranean region and Central/South America.
evidence: This describes a finding from the admixture analysis.

claim: The two main subgroups within Linf1 correspond to MON-1 and non-MON-1 zymodemes categorised by Multilocus Enzyme Electrophoresis.
source: This latter two subgroups correspond to MON-1 (31 samples of the largest subgroup) and non-MON-1 zymodemes (six samples from Europe, Turkey and Panama; Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1) categorised by Multilocus Enzyme Electrophoresis (MLEE) (Rioux et al., 1990).
evidence: This describes a finding from the phylogenetic analysis in relation to previous typing methods.

claim: Geography is not the main driver of parasite diversity across L. infantum in general nor within the globally distributed Linf1 group.
source: Therefore, geography is not the main driver of parasite diversity across L. infantum in general nor within the globally distributed Linf1 group.
evidence: This is an inference based on the phylogenetic and admixture analysis results.

claim: There is only marginal isolation-by-distance correlation within the Linf1 group (0.20, p-value<0.05, Mantel test).
source: This is also mirrored by only marginal isolation-by-distance correlations within Linf1 (0.20, p-value<0.05, Mantel test, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This describes a statistical result from the population genetic analysis.

claim: Isolation-by-distance relationships are present within the 'MON-1' subgroup of Linf1 (0.47, p-value<=0.0001, Mantel test).
source: However, IBD relationships are present within the 'MON-1' subgroup of Linf1 (0.47, p-value<=0.0001, Mantel test) and very pronounced between the non-American 'MON-1' strains (0.81, p-value<=0.0001, Mantel test, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This describes a statistical result from the population genetic analysis.

claim: Isolation-by-distance is very pronounced between the non-American 'MON-1' strains (0.81, p-value<=0.0001, Mantel test).
source: However, IBD relationships are present within the 'MON-1' subgroup of Linf1 (0.47, p-value<=0.0001, Mantel test) and very pronounced between the non-American 'MON-1' strains (0.81, p-value<=0.0001, Mantel test, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This describes a statistical result from the population genetic analysis.

claim: All 5 'MON-1' American samples formed a monophyletic sub-clade that was most closely related to parasite strains from Portugal, Spain, Italy and a single isolate from Israel suggesting a South-Western European origin of Central and South American L. infantum.
source: All 5 'MON-1' American samples formed a monophyletic sub-clade that was most closely related to parasite strains from Portugal, Spain, Italy and a single isolate from Israel suggesting a South-Western European origin of Central and South American L. infantum (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is an inference based on the phylogenetic analysis.

claim: The South-Western European origin of Central and South American L. infantum was confirmed when including another 26 L. infantum isolates sampled from three states in Brazil.
source: This result was still valid when including another 26 L. infantum isolates sampled from three states in Brazil (Carnielli et al., 2018). They all clustered in a single 'American' clade with little genetic diversity (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This describes a finding from an extended phylogenetic analysis.

claim: L. infantum in Central and Southern America is not generally monophyletic as one non-MON-1 L. infantum isolated in Panama was present in the dataset.
source: L. infantum in Central and Southern America, however, is not generally monophyletic as also one non-MON-1 L. infantum isolated in Panama was present in our dataset (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an observation from the phylogenetic analysis.

claim: For the zoonotic parasite L. infantum, 12 of 30 MON-1 strains were isolated from dogs, which is the prevalent zymodeme in dogs.
source: For the zoonotic parasite L. infantum, 12 of our 30 MON-1 strains were isolated from dogs – previously also described as the prevalent zymodeme in dogs (Pratlong et al., 2004).
evidence: This is an observation from the dataset supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: For most countries, L. infantum isolates from human and non-human hosts generally clustered by geography, supporting previous knowledge of dogs as a reservoir for human infection.
source: For most countries this included isolates from human and non-human hosts, while samples generally clustered by geography (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A). This supports previous knowledge of dogs as a reservoir for human infection (Alvar et al., 2004).
evidence: This is an observation from the phylogenetic analysis that supports previous knowledge.

claim: The remaining samples of L. infantum from Cyprus and Çukurova in Turkey are genetically more distinct and showed unusual positioning in the phylogeny close to the split between L. infantum and L. donovani.
source: In contrast to the low diversity across the wide geographical range of the core L. infantum group, Linf1, the remaining samples of L. infantum, from Cyprus and Çukurova in Turkey, are genetically more distinct and showed unusual positioning in the phylogeny close to the split between L. infantum and L. donovani.
evidence: This is an observation from the phylogenetic analysis.

claim: Samples from the Çukurova region of Turkey (CUK) are considered to be a lineage descended from a single crossing event of a strain related to the L. infantum reference strain JPCM5 and an unknown L. infantum or L. donovani strain.
source: Samples from the Çukurova region of Turkey (CUK, green) are considered to be a lineage descended from a single crossing event of a strain related to the L. infantum reference strain JPCM5 and an unknown L. infantum or L. donovani strain (Rogers et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous research study.

claim: Isolates from Cyprus (CH) are divergent from the L. infantum group and were identified as L. donovani using MLEE, but the associated pattern of markers (MON-37) has been shown to be paraphyletic.
source: Isolates from Cyprus (CH, grey) are also divergent from the L. infantum group: these parasites were identified as L. donovani using MLEE, but the associated pattern of markers (MON-37) has been shown to be paraphyletic (Alam et al., 2009), so its species identity might be debateable.
evidence: This is an observation from the phylogenetic analysis supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Two Cypriot isolates (CH32 and CH34) are admixed between the Çukurova and remaining Cypriot strains.
source: Our data suggest that the two slightly different Cypriot isolates (CH32 and CH34) are admixed between the Çukurova and remaining Cypriot strains.
evidence: This is an inference based on the admixture and phylogenetic analysis.

claim: Two more isolates (MAM and EP; from Brazil and Turkey) are both highly divergent from any other isolates in the phylogeny and appeared to be admixed between the Linf1 group and other lineages.
source: Two more isolates (MAM and EP; from Brazil and Turkey) are both highly divergent from any other isolates in the phylogeny, and appeared to be admixed between the Linf1 group and other lineages.
evidence: This is an observation from the phylogenetic and admixture analysis.

claim: There is no overall isolation-by-distance relationship across all L. infantum samples (−0.12, ns., Mantel test).
source: As expected from the relatively high divergence of the CUK and Cypriot clades that have their origin from the centre of the sampling range, there is no overall IBD relationship across all L. infantum samples (−0.12, ns., Mantel test, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This describes a statistical result from the population genetic analysis.

claim: In contrast to L. donovani, the majority of L. infantum shows little diversity, but diverse strains can co-localise in the case of non-MON-1 strains and can have diversified by hybridisation in case of the CUK strains.
source: This suggests that in contrast to L. donovani, the majority of L. infantum shows little diversity, but diverse strains can co-localise in the case of non-MON-1 strains (see also Guerbouj et al., 2001) and can have diversified by hybridisation in case of the CUK strains.
evidence: This is an inference based on the phylogenetic and diversity analysis, supported by a citation.

claim: Extensive variation in chromosome copy number was observed in isolated strains in vitro, inferred from read coverage depth, with the pattern of variation being incongruent with the genome-wide phylogeny.
source: We observed extensive variation in chromosome copy number in our isolated strains in vitro, inferred from read coverage depth, with the pattern of variation being incongruent with the genome-wide phylogeny (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes a finding from the aneuploidy analysis.

claim: Aneuploidy patterns are known to vary over very short time scales, even within strains and upon changing environments.
source: Aneuploidy patterns are known to vary over very short time scales, even within strains and upon changing environments (Sterkers et al., 2011; Dumetz et al., 2017; Lachaud et al., 2014), although consistent patterns of aneuploidy have been observed within small groups of closely related cultured field isolates (Imamura et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to research studies.

claim: Consistent patterns of aneuploidy have been observed within small groups of closely related cultured field isolates.
source: Aneuploidy patterns are known to vary over very short time scales, even within strains and upon changing environments (Sterkers et al., 2011; Dumetz et al., 2017; Lachaud et al., 2014), although consistent patterns of aneuploidy have been observed within small groups of closely related cultured field isolates (Imamura et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a research study.

claim: The majority of chromosomes had a median somy of two across isolates, apart from chromosomes 8, 9 and 23 and chromosome 31 with a median somy of three and four, respectively.
source: As expected, the majority of chromosomes had a median somy of two across isolates, apart from chromosomes 8, 9 and 23 and chromosome 31 with a median somy of three and four, respectively (Figure 2A,C, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This describes a finding from the aneuploidy analysis.

claim: Trisomy was widespread with all chromosomes being overall trisomic in at least two isolates (2%) and at least half of all chromosomes were trisomic in ≥ 28 isolates (19%).
source: However, trisomy was widespread with all chromosomes being overall trisomic in at least two isolates (2%) and at least half of all chromosomes were trisomic in ≥ 28 isolates (19%).
evidence: This describes a finding from the aneuploidy analysis.

claim: Monosomy was rare with only four chromosomes having somy of one in a single isolate each.
source: In contrast, monosomy was rare – with only four chromosomes having somy of one in a single isolate each.
evidence: This describes a finding from the aneuploidy analysis.

claim: Chromosome 31 was unusual in being dominantly tetrasomic (81% of samples) with no somy levels below three observed.
source: As previously reported for Leishmania (e.g. Akopyants et al., 2009; Downing et al., 2011; Imamura et al., 2016 ), chromosome 31 was unusual in being dominantly tetrasomic (81% of samples) and we observed no somy levels below three.
evidence: This describes a finding from the aneuploidy analysis, supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Much of the aneuploidy pattern (general disomy with occasional trisomy and sporadic higher dosage for most chromosomes) was consistent across the four largest groups, as was the high dosage of chromosome 31.
source: Much of this pattern – general disomy, with occasional trisomy and sporadic higher dosage for most chromosomes – was consistent across the four largest groups, as was the high dosage of chromosome 31 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This describes a finding from the aneuploidy analysis.

claim: Chromosome 23 showed a tendency to trisomy in all four largest groups, and chromosomes 8 and 9 were dominantly trisomic in three of the groups.
source: Similarly, chromosome 23 showed a tendency to trisomy in all four groups, and chromosomes 8 and 9 were dominantly trisomic in three of the groups.
evidence: This describes a finding from the aneuploidy analysis.

claim: Copy number variability for each chromosome was positively correlated between the four largest groups.
source: Copy number variability for each chromosome was estimated by the standard deviation (sd) in somy and was positively correlated between the four largest groups (Figure 2B).
evidence: This describes a finding from the aneuploidy analysis.

claim: Correlations of chromosome copy number variability were much higher between three groups from diverse sampling locations, while correlations to the CUK group were lower, suggesting a distinct pattern of aneuploidy variability in this group.
source: Correlations were much higher between three groups from diverse sampling locations, while correlations to the CUK group sampled in the Çukurova province were lower, suggesting a distinct pattern of aneuploidy variability in this group – perhaps due to its hybrid origin (Rogers et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference based on the aneuploidy analysis, with a citation to support the hybrid origin.

claim: Some chromosomes have higher propensities for chromosome aneuploidy turnover than others, with the top five chromosomes being 23, 5, 8, 6 and 26.
source: A few chromosomes including 19, 27, 28 and 34 showed almost no variation, while several chromosomes showed very high variation in chromosome copy number with the top five chromosomes being 23, 5, 8, 6 and 26 (Figure 2C). This indicated that some chromosomes have higher propensities for chromosome aneuploidy turnover than others.
evidence: This is an inference based on the aneuploidy analysis.

claim: Samples varied greatly in genome-wide heterozygosity: 70% of the isolates showed extremely low heterozygosity (<0.004; corresponding to between 23 and 2057 heterozygous sites per sample, median = 80).
source: Samples varied greatly in genome-wide heterozygosity: 70% of the isolates in our collection showed extremely low heterozygosity (<0.004; see Materials and methods) corresponding to between 23 and 2057 (median = 80) heterozygous sites per sample.
evidence: This describes a finding from the heterozygosity analysis.

claim: The remaining high-heterozygosity samples largely showed heterozygosities up to ~0.02 (equivalent to 15,281 heterozygous sites per sample) with a few outliers exceeding this threshold and reaching a heterozygosity of 0.065 in one isolate (MAM, 50,543 heterozygous sites).
source: The remaining high-heterozygosity samples largely showed heterozygosities up to ~0.02 (equivalent to 15,281 heterozygous sites per sample) with a few outliers exceeding this threshold and reaching a heterozygosity of 0.065 in one isolate (MAM, 50,543 heterozygous sites) (Figure 3A).
evidence: This describes a finding from the heterozygosity analysis.

claim: For almost all isolates the majority of genome-wide 10 kb windows had almost no heterozygous sites: only 11 isolates had a median count of heterozygous sites per window greater than zero.
source: For almost all isolates the majority of genome-wide 10 kb windows had almost no heterozygous sites: only 11 isolates had a median count of heterozygous sites per window greater than zero (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes a finding from the heterozygosity analysis.

claim: The predominant homozygosity for the majority of isolates of the L. donovani complex is in striking contrast to expectations for sexual populations under Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium or for clonally reproducing populations.
source: This predominant homozygosity for the majority of isolates of the L. donovani complex was in striking contrast to expectations for sexual populations under Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, or for clonally reproducing populations: clonal reproduction is expected to increase heterozygosity, as single mutations cannot be assorted to form novel homozygous genotypes (Balloux et al., 2003; De Meeûs et al., 2006; Weir et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an observation with an inference based on population genetic theory, supported by citations.

claim: Most main groups were dominated by samples of low heterozygosity, with the exception of the Ldon3 group and the CUK group of hybrid L. infantum isolates.
source: Most main groups were dominated by samples of low heterozygosity, with the exception of the Ldon3 group and the CUK group of hybrid L. infantum isolates (Rogers et al., 2014).
evidence: This describes a finding from the heterozygosity analysis, with a citation for the CUK group.

claim: Other high-heterozygosity isolates mainly appeared in positions intermediate between large groups in the phylogeny and showed mixed ancestry in the admixture analysis, leading to the hypothesis that they represent recent hybrids between distinct, well-differentiated populations.
source: Other high-heterozygosity isolates mainly appeared in positions intermediate between large groups in the phylogeny, and showed mixed ancestry in the admixture analysis (e.g. isolates MAM, EP, CH32, CH34, GE, LEM3472, LRC-L740; Figure 1A), leading us to hypothesise that they represent recent hybrids between the distinct, well-differentiated populations.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the phylogenetic, admixture, and heterozygosity analyses.

claim: The low heterozygosity together with strong genetic signatures of inbreeding in Leishmania had previously been identified using MLST and microsatellite data and has generally been attributed to extensive selfing between cells from the same clone.
source: The low heterozygosity together with strong genetic signatures of inbreeding in Leishmania had previously been identified using MLST and microsatellite data, and has generally been attributed to extensive selfing between cells from the same clone (Ramírez and Llewellyn, 2014; Rougeron et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: An alternative explanation for low heterozygosity could be that frequent aneuploidy turnover reduces within-cell heterozygosity if an alternate haplotype is lost during somy reduction.
source: However, an alternative explanation could be that frequent aneuploidy turnover also reduces within-cell heterozygosity if an alternate haplotype is lost during somy reduction (Sterkers et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Linear regressions for different groups showed negative slopes for three of seven groups but only the slope for the Ldon3 group was significant after multiple testing correction when testing whether chromosome-specific variation in somy is negatively correlated with chromosome-specific sample heterozygosity.
source: Linear regressions for the different groups showed negative slopes for three of seven groups but only the slope for the Ldon3 group was significant after multiple testing correction (Figure 3B).
evidence: This describes a statistical result from the analysis of the relationship between aneuploidy and heterozygosity.

claim: For four groups (Ldon1, Ldon2, Ldon5 and Linf1) where the regression slope between chromosome-specific somy variation and heterozygosity was almost zero, the chromosomes were almost completely homozygous which might make potential effects undetectable.
source: For the four groups, Ldon1, Ldon2, Ldon5 and Linf1, where the regression slope was almost zero, the chromosomes were almost completely homozygous which might make potential effects undetectable (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is an inference based on the analysis results.

claim: The data for the remaining groups is in accordance with a reduction in heterozygosity with aneuploidy turnover.
source: The data for the remaining groups is in accordance with a reduction in heterozygosity with aneuploidy turnover.
evidence: This is an inference based on the analysis results.

claim: To establish presence and effect sizes of a reduction in heterozygosity due to aneuploidy turnover, direct experiments and more accurate estimates of aneuploidy turnover are needed, particularly using in vivo parasites.
source: However, to establish presence and effect sizes of a reduction in heterozygosity due to aneuploidy turnover direct experiments and more accurate estimates of aneuploidy turnover are needed, particularly using in vivo parasites.
evidence: This is a statement about what is needed for future research.

claim: 28 of the 46 high heterozygosity isolates appeared to represent genuine hybrid lineages, and for 17 of these, likely parents could be assigned.
source: 28 of the 46 high heterozygosity isolates appeared to represent genuine hybrid lineages (rows B1, B2 and B4 in Table 1), and for 17 of these, likely parents could be assigned (row B2 in Table 1).
evidence: This describes a finding from the detailed hybrid analysis.

claim: Two Cypriot isolates (CH32 and CH34) showed patches of homozygosity closely related to the other Cypriot isolates and the Turkish CUK hybrids, likely representing hybrids closely related to the CUK hybrids but derived from an independent hybridisation event.
source: Additionally, two Cypriot isolates (CH32 and CH34) showed patches of homozygosity closely related to the other Cypriot isolates and the Turkish CUK hybrids (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A). Therefore, CH32 and CH34 likely represent hybrids closely related to the CUK hybrids, but clearly derived from an independent hybridisation event to the CUK population itself (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is an inference based on the genomic analysis of heterozygosity patterns.

claim: Another Turkish isolate (EP) appeared to have a similar evolutionary history to the CUK hybrids with putative parental strains from the Linf1 and the CUK hybrids.
source: Another Turkish isolate (EP) appeared to have a similar evolutionary history with putative parental strains from the Linf1 and the CUK hybrids (Figure 4).
evidence: This is an inference based on the genomic analysis of heterozygosity patterns.

claim: For the EP isolate, there were entire homozygous chromosomes that resembled either of the two putative parental groups (chromosomes 4, 12, 22 and 32 for one and 11, 23 and 24 for the other parent).
source: In contrast to previous hybrids, for EP, there were entire homozygous chromosomes that resembled either of the two putative parental groups (chromosomes 4, 12, 22 and 32 for one and 11, 23 and 24 for the other parent; Figure 4).
evidence: This describes a finding from the genomic analysis of the EP isolate.

claim: Phylogenetic analysis of the kDNA maxicircles showed that the EP isolate has identical sequences to the Cypriot hybrid samples (CH23 and CH34).
source: Phylogenetic analysis of the kDNA maxicircles further showed identical sequences to the Cypriot hybrid samples (CH23 and CH34, Figure 4—figure supplements 3, 4, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This describes a finding from the phylogenetic analysis of maxicircle DNA.

claim: On two chromosomes (5 and 31) in the EP isolate, allele frequency distributions were not compatible with a single, clonal population of cells suggesting the presence of a second but very closely related low frequency clone in this sample.
source: Additionally, on two chromosomes, 5 and 31, allele frequency distributions in the EP isolate were not compatible with a single, clonal population of cells suggesting the presence of a second but very closely related low frequency clone in this sample (Figure 4—figure supplements 2, 5).
evidence: This is an inference based on the allele frequency analysis.

claim: Two isolates from East Africa (GE and LEM3472) and one from Israel (LRC-L740) showed discrete patches of heterozygous and homozygous variants and appeared admixed between the North Ethiopia/Sudan group (Ldon3) and the L. donovani group present in the Middle East (Ldon4).
source: We also saw discrete patches of heterozygous and homozygous variants in two isolates from East Africa (GE and LEM3472) and one from Israel (LRC-L740) that did not fit into any of the main L. donovani groups. These isolates appeared admixed between the North Ethiopia/Sudan group (Ldon3) and the L. donovani group present in the Middle East (Ldon4) (Figures 1A and 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This describes a finding from the genomic and admixture analysis.

claim: For sample GE, kDNA confirmed that one putative parent came from the Ldon3 group.
source: For sample GE, kDNA further confirmed that one putative parent came from the Ldon3 group (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This describes a finding from the phylogenetic analysis of maxicircle DNA.

claim: All the isolates from the Ldon3 group were highly heterozygous and so potentially hybrids, but other possible origins for this heterozygosity cannot be excluded.
source: All the isolates from the Ldon3 group, were also highly heterozygous and so potentially hybrids, but we cannot exclude other possible origins for this heterozygosity (Figures 3A and 4 , Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Table 1).
evidence: This is a statement acknowledging uncertainty about the interpretation of heterozygosity.

claim: For 12 isolates, many of the heterozygous sites were present at extreme (high/low) allele frequencies or at multiple intermediate frequencies, incompatible with the allele frequencies expected based on chromosomal somy, suggesting these isolates represent a mixture of multiple cell clones.
source: Unexpectedly, for 12 of the remaining isolates (rows B3 – B5 in Table 1), many of the heterozygous sites were present at extreme (high/low) allele frequencies (11 isolates) or at multiple intermediate frequencies (isolate GILANI), incompatible with the allele frequencies expected based on chromosomal somy (Figure 4—figure supplements 2, 5). We suspect that these isolates represent a mixture of multiple cell clones.
evidence: This is an inference based on the allele frequency analysis.

claim: The MAM isolate had the highest heterozygosity in the collection with only 178 homozygous differences to the JPCM5 reference but 50,534 heterozygous sites, with a frequency of the reference allele of ~0.92 across all chromosomes.
source: The MAM isolate had the highest heterozygosity in our collection: it only had 178 homozygous differences to the JPCM5 reference, but 50,534 heterozygous sites, with a frequency of the reference allele of ~0.92 across all chromosomes (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This describes a finding from the heterozygosity and allele frequency analysis.

claim: The MAM sample is most likely a mixture between a JPCM5-like L. infantum strain at high (~0.92) and an L. donovani related to Ldon5 at low (0.08) sample frequency.
source: We concluded that the MAM sample is most likely a mixture between a JPCM5-like L. infantum strain at high (~0.92) and an L. donovani related to Ldon5 at low (0.08) sample frequency.
evidence: This is an inference based on the phylogenetic and allele frequency analysis.

claim: Several isolates within L. donovani groups (BPK157A1 in Ldon1, Malta33 and GILANI in Ldon3, SUKKAR2 and BUMM3 in Ldon4 and LRC-L53 in Ldon5) appeared to be mixtures of two clones from within the respective group.
source: Similarly, the few heterozygous isolates within several L. donovani groups, BPK157A1 in Ldon1, Malta33 and GILANI in Ldon3, SUKKAR2 and BUMM3 in Ldon4 and LRC-L53 in Ldon5 (Figure 3A) all appeared to be mixtures of two clones from within the respective group (Figure 4—figure supplement 9) apart from GILANI, which might be a more complex mixture (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an inference based on the phylogenetic and allele frequency analysis.

claim: One isolate (BPK157A1) was re-grown from a single cell prior to sequencing, so it cannot be certain that the observed variants are due to a mixture of clones.
source: However, as one isolate from this subset (BPK157A1) was re-grown from a single cell prior to sequencing (Supplementary file 1), we cannot be sure that these variants are due to a mixture of clones.
evidence: This is a statement acknowledging uncertainty about the interpretation of the data.

claim: Highly heterozygous isolates from L. infantum (ISS174, ISS2426, ISS2429 and Inf152 in Linf1) had skewed allele frequency distributions and therefore likely represent either mixed clone isolates or samples that have evolved significant diversity during in vitro growth.
source: Highly heterozygous isolates from L. infantum (ISS174, ISS2426, ISS2429 and Inf152 in Linf1) also had skewed allele frequency distributions Figure 4—figure supplements 2, 11), and therefore likely represent either mixed clone isolates or samples that have evolved significant diversity during in vitro growth.
evidence: This is an inference based on the allele frequency analysis.

claim: Samples ISS174, ISS2426 and ISS2429 showed a strong positive correlation of chromosomal heterozygosity and somy not found in any other samples, suggesting these isolates may have accumulated substantial numbers of new mutations most likely while maintaining relatively stable chromosome copy number during in vitro culture.
source: Samples, ISS174, ISS2426 and ISS2429, showed a strong positive correlation of chromosomal heterozygosity and somy not found in any other samples (Figure 4—figure supplement 12). We speculate that these isolates may have accumulated substantial numbers of new mutations most likely while maintaining relatively stable chromosome copy number during in vitro culture.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed correlation.

claim: Sexual recombination is not obligate in the Leishmania lifecycle and appears to be rare in many natural populations.
source: Sexual recombination is not obligate in the Leishmania lifecycle and appears to be rare in many natural populations (Imamura et al., 2016; Ramírez and Llewellyn, 2014; Rougeron et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to research studies.

claim: Patterns of linkage disequilibrium (LD) between Leishmania populations were examined as a clue to the frequency of sexual recombination.
source: We thus examined patterns of linkage disequilibrium (LD) between Leishmania populations as a clue to the frequency of sexual recombination, bearing in mind that LD can be affected by underlying population structure.
evidence: This describes the approach used in the study.

claim: LD estimates depend on the frequency of recombination, the population size, demographic history and the size of sample taken from the population.
source: LD estimates further depend on the frequency of recombination, the population size, demographic history (Slatkin, 1994) and the size of sample taken from the population (see also Figure 5A versus Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is established population genetic knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Strong differences between groups in LD decay with genomic distance were found when larger groups were subsampled to identical group sizes.
source: We subsampled larger groups to identical group sizes and found strong differences between groups in LD decay with genomic distance (Figure 5A).
evidence: This describes a finding from the linkage disequilibrium analysis.

claim: Linkage was strongest in the Ldon2 group with mean LD estimates around 0.9 regardless of genomic distance between SNPs, even when comparing sites on different chromosomes.
source: Linkage was strongest in the Ldon2 group with mean LD estimates around 0.9 regardless of genomic distance between SNPs, even when comparing sites on different chromosomes.
evidence: This describes a finding from the linkage disequilibrium analysis.

claim: The L. infantum groups (Linf1 and the CUK samples) started with high mean LD values for 1 kb distances above 0.9 and 0.8, respectively, and dropped to ~0.5 for 100 kb distances and to ~0.4 and ~0.3 between chromosomes.
source: The L. infantum groups (Linf1 and the CUK samples) started with high mean LD values for 1 kb distances above 0.9 and 0.8, respectively, and dropped to ~0.5 for 100 kb distances and to ~0.4 and ~0.3 between chromosomes.
evidence: This describes a finding from the linkage disequilibrium analysis.

claim: Ldon3 and Ldon5 groups had the lowest LD estimates: at up to 1 kb distances LD had mean values of ~0.8 and 0.6 for Ldon3 and Ldon5, respectively, and dropped to ~0.2 for distances ≥ 50 kb in both groups and remained at those levels between chromosomes.
source: Ldon3 and Ldon5 groups had the lowest LD estimates: at up to 1 kb distances LD had mean values of ~0.8 and 0.6 for Ldon3 and Ldon5, respectively, and dropped to ~0.2 for distances ≥ 50 kb in both groups and remained at those levels between chromosomes.
evidence: This describes a finding from the linkage disequilibrium analysis.

claim: For Ldon1, the mean LD had a flat distribution with genomic distance like the Ldon2 group but at a much lower LD level, and showed significant variation between 3 subsamples.
source: All of these trends were relatively consistent among three independent subsamples from each of the larger groups, but the pattern was more complex for Ldon1. Here, the mean LD had a flat distribution with genomic distance like the Ldon2 group but at a much lower LD level, and showed significant variation between 3 subsamples (Figure 5B): two of the three subsamples showed low but very variable LD, and the third showed consistently high LD with distance.
evidence: This describes a finding from the linkage disequilibrium analysis.

claim: Low LD replicates in Ldon1 were based on samples with a greatly reduced number of within-replicate SNPs (683 and 685 in R1 and R3 versus 23,303 SNPs in replicate R2).
source: Low LD replicates were based on samples with a greatly reduced number of within-replicate SNPs (683 and 685 in R1 and R3 versus 23,303 SNPs in replicate R2).
evidence: This describes a finding from the linkage disequilibrium analysis.

claim: In the low LD replicates of Ldon1, the majority of SNPs were singletons or present in only two copies, while in replicate R2 the majority of minor alleles were present at four copies.
source: In the low LD replicates the majority of SNPs were singletons or present in only two copies, while in replicate R2 the majority of minor alleles were present at four copies (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This describes a finding from the allele frequency analysis.

claim: The substructure described for samples from the Indian subcontinent is responsible for varying LD estimates of the subsamples in Ldon1, with low LD replicates due to sampling only closely-related subgroups that only differ in a small number of isolate-specific variants that are most parsimoniously described by recent mutations.
source: We conclude that the substructure described for samples from the Indian subcontinent (Imamura et al., 2016) is responsible for varying LD estimates of the subsamples, with low LD replicates due to sampling only closely-related subgroups that only differ in a small number of isolate-specific variants that are most parsimoniously described by recent mutations (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is an inference based on the linkage disequilibrium and allele frequency analysis, supported by a citation.

claim: A gradual decrease of LD with distance is interpreted as a signal of frequent recombination occurring in those populations.
source: While the level of LD in a population cannot be used to directly quantify the frequency of recombination due to the contribution of demographic factors, we interpret a gradual decrease of LD with distance as a signal of frequent recombination occurring in those populations.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the linkage disequilibrium results.

claim: The groups also differed in their allele frequency distributions (site frequency spectra, SFS).
source: The groups also differed in their allele frequency distributions (i.e. the site frequency spectra, SFS).
evidence: This describes a finding from the allele frequency analysis.

claim: Most of the groups (Ldon1, Ldon2, Ldon5 and Linf1) were dominated by low frequency variants.
source: While we would not predict Leishmania populations to exactly follow these expectations, most of the groups (Ldon1, Ldon2, Ldon5 and Linf1) were dominated by low frequency variants (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This describes a finding from the allele frequency analysis.

claim: Intermediate frequency variants were frequent in Ldon3 and even dominated variation in the L. infantum CUK samples.
source: In contrast, intermediate frequency variants were frequent in Ldon3 and even dominated variation in the L. infantum CUK samples.
evidence: This describes a finding from the allele frequency analysis.

claim: The CUK group had been suggested to have largely expanded clonally from a single hybridisation event between diverse strains with little subsequent hybridisation, which might explain why polymorphic sites generated by the hybridisation of diverse strains and common to the majority of samples can be at intermediate population frequency.
source: The CUK group had been suggested to have largely expanded clonally from a single hybridisation event between diverse strains with little subsequent hybridisation (Rogers et al., 2014). This scenario might explain why polymorphic sites, generated by the hybridisation of diverse strains and common to the majority of samples can be at intermediate population frequency.
evidence: This is an inference based on the allele frequency analysis and a previous study.

claim: The CUK group history agrees with stronger LD over short distances due to shared blocks that may be broken up by rare subsequent hybridisation and recombination events.
source: This group history also agrees with stronger LD over short distances due to shared blocks that may be broken up by rare subsequent hybridisation and recombination events.

claim: For the Ldon3 group, increased intermediate frequency alleles combined with a strong decline of LD with distance might suggest that old variants are segregating in the group at high frequencies, due to relatively frequent hybridisation between clones within this group.
source: For the Ldon3 group increased intermediate frequency alleles combined with a strong decline of LD with distance might suggest that old variants are segregating in the group at high frequencies, due to relatively frequent hybridisation between clones within this group.

claim: Most SNP sites segregating within each pair of groups were found to be population-specific (FST = 1) in 10 out of 15 pairs.
source: Most SNP sites segregating within each pair of groups were found to be population-specific, that is FST = 1, in 10 out of 15 pairs (Figure 6A).

claim: Most groups are well differentiated from each other with limited gene flow between them.
source: This confirmed that most groups are well differentiated from each other with limited gene flow between them.

claim: Between 6,769 and 26,145 potentially differentially fixed 'marker' SNPs were identified for each group.

claim: 11,228 SNPs were differentially fixed supporting the species split between L. infantum and L. donovani.
source: Despite this differentiation, many variants remained that were fixed in combinations of groups. Most of these SNPs supported the species split, between L. infantum and L. donovani, with 11,228 differentially fixed SNPs (Figure 6C).
